column4: text
Wind's backed around northwest, Captain. She's starting to roll some.
column5: From the chart room behind you. Calm, a professional. Raising his voice a little over the wind.

column4: I feel it. Hold her on one-three-zero. We'll be in the lee of Whitefish by suppertime.
column5: Unhurried. You've been doing this for forty years.

column4: Aye. Weather office went to storm warnings this morning. All of Lake Superior.
Fitzgerald, this is the Anderson. You on here?
column5: The captain of the ship ten miles astern. Old friend. Relaxed.

column4: Go ahead, Anderson.
column5: Holding the handset. Clipped radio manner.

column4: We're seeing gusts to fifty back here. Seas twelve, fifteen feet and building. How's she riding?
Rolling some. Nothing she hasn't done before. We're going to haul on down past Caribou and run for Whitefish.
Roger that. We'll be right behind you. Anderson clear.
Engine room. She's running fine, Captain, but the wheel's coming out of the water when the stern lifts. Shaft's racing on us.
column5: Phone line, engine noise behind him. Practical, a bit gruff.

column4: What was that? You feel that, Captain?
Felt like she bumped something. We're awful close to that shoal off Caribou.
Captain, deck watch. There's a fence rail down on the starboard side. And two of the vent caps are gone off the ballast tanks.
column5: Shouting into the phone, wind howling. Young-ish.

column4: And Captain... she's got a list on her. To starboard. I can see it from back here.
Anderson, this is the Fitzgerald. I have a fence rail down, two vents lost or damaged, and a list. I'm checking down. Will you stay by me till I get to Whitefish?
column5: Measured, controlled. This is serious but you won't let it show.

column4: Charlie on that, Fitzgerald. Do you have your pumps going?
column5: A beat of concern under the calm.

column4: Yes. Both of them.
Starting them now.
column5: Short. A little irritated with yourself.

column4: We'll stay with you. Anderson standing by on sixteen.
Fitzgerald, Anderson. You're riding awful low from what I can see back here. Everything all right up there?
Captain, I've lost the radar. Both sets. The picture's just gone.
column5: Coming from the radar. Flat disbelief.

column4: Must have carried away the scanners up top.
Anderson, this is the Fitzgerald. I've lost both radars. Can you keep track of me and give me some navigational help?
We'll do that, Fitzgerald. We've got you on the scope, about ten miles ahead of us. We'll keep you posted.
Fitzgerald, this is the Anderson. How are you making out up there?
Fitzgerald, Anderson. You're bearing one-four-zero from us. Whitefish is about twenty-five miles off your bow. Steer about one-four-one.
One-four-one. Thanks, Anderson.
Captain, I can't get the Whitefish beacon on the direction finder. Nothing at all. And there's no light.
Coast Guard Sault, this is the Edmund Fitzgerald. Is the light and the radio beacon at Whitefish Point working?
Fitzgerald, Coast Guard Group Sault. Our monitor shows the Whitefish beacon is off the air. Power's out on the point. We'll get somebody on it. Over.
Roger. Fitzgerald out.
Any vessel near Whitefish Point, this is the Edmund Fitzgerald. Is the light at Whitefish working?
Fitzgerald, this is the Avafors. We're just coming around Whitefish now. The light's out and the beacon's out too. It's a mess out here.
column5: A Lakes pilot on a foreign ship. Plain-spoken Midwesterner.

column4: I've got a bad list. Lost both radars. And I'm taking heavy seas over the deck. One of the worst seas I've ever been in.
column5: Tired. The truest thing you've said all day.

column4: We're getting it too. Seas are twenty-five feet out here. Good luck to you, Fitzgerald.
Don't allow nobody on deck.
column5: Turning away from the handset, to someone in the pilothouse. Sharp.

column4: Fitzgerald, Avafors. Heard you asking about Whitefish. The light's back on now, but the beacon's still out. How are you making out?
Captain, engine room. Pumps are working hard. Whatever's coming in, it's coming in steady.
Captain! That one came clean over the hatches! Whole deck aft is under water!
She's slow coming back up from these, Captain.
column5: Quiet, close by. Watching the clinometer.

column4: Sécurité, sécurité, sécurité. This is Coast Guard Group Sault Ste. Marie. Storm warnings remain in effect for all of Lake Superior. Northwest winds fifty to sixty knots, higher in gusts. Waves eighteen to twenty-five feet. All vessels seek shelter. Sault Coast Guard out.
column5: Pronounced "say-cure-ee-tay". Official broadcast, flat and deliberate.

column4: Captain... we've got water in the tunnel. Not much yet. Pumps are keeping up. For now.
column5: The first crack in his voice.

column4: Fitzgerald, Anderson. We just took two big ones over the stern. Water up over the hatch covers. Watch yourself, they're headed your way.
Roger. We'll watch for them.
Whitefish is about fifteen miles off, Captain. We'll be in the lee inside the hour.
Fitzgerald, this is the Anderson. Have you checked down? There's a target nineteen miles ahead of us, you'll clear it. By the way, how are you making out with your problems?
column5: Routine. Friendly. He has no idea.

column4: We are holding our own.
column5: The last words. Plain, steady, almost offhand. Do several takes.

column4: Okay, fine. I'll be talking to you later.
Captain, she's not coming up—
column5: Cut off mid-word. Do not finish the sentence.

column4: Engine room, start the ballast pumps. Both of them.
Engine room, secure the ballast pumps.
Have somebody sound the tanks and let me know.
Deck watch. What's it look like back there?
Pass the word. Nobody goes out on deck. Nobody.
Chief, how's she running?
Mate, what have you got on the radar?
Wheelsman, take her. Hold her steady on this heading.
Where are we, Mate?
Pass the word. Everybody into their life jackets.
column5: Quiet and very calm. You don't want to frighten anyone.

column4: Galley, send some coffee up to the pilothouse.
Both pumps, aye. Pumping now.
Securing the pumps... aye, Captain.
Tanks are dry, Captain. Nothing in them you wouldn't expect.
Taking some water in the starboard tanks, Captain. Two, three feet.
There's water in more tanks than I'd like, Captain. Six, eight feet in some. Pumps aren't gaining.
It's coming in faster than we can get it out, Captain.
All secure, Captain. Hatch clamps are holding. Lot of water coming over, but she's tight.
Fence rail's down on the starboard side, couple of vent caps gone. Still taking water over the deck.
I can't hardly see the deck aft, Captain. It's green water over the hatches every other sea.
Aye, Captain. I'll tell the galley and the watch.
Steady as she goes down here, Captain. Shaft races when the stern lifts, but she's holding.
She's fine down here. I can feel that list though. Everything's leaning.
We're making turns. Don't know how much longer the pumps can keep up.
Anderson's about ten miles astern. Caribou's off to the west. Nothing else out here but us.
Nothing, Captain. Both screens are dead.
Steady as she goes, aye, Captain.
You have the wheel, Captain.
Still a long way off, Captain. Forty miles to Whitefish, give or take.
About thirty miles to Whitefish, Captain.
Twenty miles to Whitefish, Captain. Getting there.
Fifteen miles off Whitefish. Almost to the lee.
Captain, we're well off the course line. Whitefish is the other way.
...Aye, Captain.
column5: A long pause first. He understands what it means.

column4: I'll send the porter up. If he can make it along the tunnel.
Anderson, Fitzgerald. How's it look back there?
Rough, but we're making it. You're about ten miles ahead of us.
Taking green water over the deck back here. You're still showing ten miles ahead.
Worst I've ever seen it. Hang in there, Fitzgerald.
Coast Guard Sault, Fitzgerald. What's the latest on the weather?
Fitzgerald, Sault Coast Guard. Storm warnings in effect. Northwest winds fifty knots, gusts to seventy. Seas fifteen to twenty-five feet. Over.
Mayday, mayday, mayday. This is the Edmund Fitzgerald, northwest of Whitefish Point. We're taking on water with a heavy list. Request assistance.
column5: The call nobody on the real ship ever made. Steady but urgent.

column4: Edmund Fitzgerald, Coast Guard Group Sault. We copy your Mayday. Say the nature of your distress. Over.
Fitzgerald, Sault. We have nothing that can get out to you in these seas. We're asking for an aircraft out of Traverse City. Nearest vessel to you is the Anderson. Over.
Fitzgerald, Anderson. We heard that. We're coming up behind you as fast as she'll go.
Fitzgerald, Coast Guard. We copy your Mayday. Aircraft is being readied. Hold on, Fitzgerald.

This is WGLR, twelve-thirty on your dial. The National Weather Service has upgraded gale warnings to storm warnings for all of Lake Superior. Northwest winds thirty-five to fifty knots, waves eight to fifteen feet.
column5: 1970s small-town AM newsreader. Warm baritone, slightly fast.

column4: Here's the marine forecast. Storm warnings, Lake Superior. Northwest winds forty-five to sixty knots tonight. Waves twelve to eighteen feet, occasionally higher. Snow showers, visibility under a mile at times.
Around the Soo this afternoon, high winds have torn down power lines and toppled trees. Highway crews are asking folks to stay home if they can.
Power is out across parts of Chippewa County this evening as the storm moves through. Utility crews say it may be morning before everyone's back on.
The Weather Service says the worst of it should come through tonight, with winds easing tomorrow afternoon. Stay warm out there, and keep a thought for the boys out on the lake.
Eight-fifty, CKSM, Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario. It's a wild one out there tonight, folks. Here's a little something to keep the lights on.
column5: Canadian radio DJ, cheerful, a little hokey.

column4: CKSM. Phone lines are lit up tonight, half of you have lost power and the other half are asking us about it. Hang in there.
You're listening to the late show. Got a request in tonight for a song about a big ore boat on Superior. Looked all through the stacks. Can't find it anywhere.
column5: Late-night DJ, soft, a little uncanny. Slow.

column4: Maybe nobody's written it yet. Here's something quiet instead. For everybody out on the big lake tonight.

column1: # ---- Caribou Island: the wheelsman takes over if you steer for it ----

column4: That's Caribou Island, Captain. Off the starboard bow, low and dark. We'll leave it well to starboard.
column5: Pointing out the window. Matter of fact.

column4: I have the wheel, Captain! Caribou's close aboard. Bringing her hard around.
column5: Sharp, loud. The one time he raises his voice.

column4: You have the wheel. Hold her off it.
She's clear, Captain. Steadying up on one-four-one for Whitefish. Your wheel.

column1: # ---- off the course line: the Anderson notices ----

column4: Fitzgerald, Anderson. I show you well off the line to Whitefish. You having steering trouble up there?
Negative, Anderson. Coming back around to one-four-one.
Fitzgerald, Anderson. You're still wandering. Whitefish is one-four-one from you. Come on back to it, Captain. It's no night to be out there on your own.
Roger, Anderson. Coming right.

column1: # ---- the watch passes: things people say when nothing much is happening ----

column4: Glass is still dropping. Twenty-nine twenty-four and going.
Lowest I've seen it on this lake.
She's riding it, Captain. Heavy, but she's riding it.
column5: Reassuring himself as much as you.

column4: Snow's closing in again. Can't see the stern from here.
Those hatch clamps had better be holding. That's green water going over them.
Another couple of hours and we'll have Whitefish under our lee.
She wants to fall off to starboard every time one comes under the quarter.
Holding one-four-one, Captain. Give or take.
Felt that one through the wheel.
Engine room. All's well down here, Captain. She's turning a hundred and twelve and burning clean.
Bridge, engine room. We've got water coming down the tunnel from somewhere forward. Pumps are keeping up. For now.
column5: Measured. The "for now" is the point.

column4: Bridge, after house. Spray's freezing on the rails back here. Nobody's going out on that deck.
Fitzgerald, Anderson. How's she riding up there?
Riding heavy, Anderson. Taking some over the bow, but she's doing fine.
Fitzgerald, Anderson. We just took a big one over the stern. Lost a lifeboat cover. You watch yourself up there.
Roger that, Anderson. Fitzgerald out.
Dark as the inside of a cow out there. Not a light anywhere.
We'd be raising Whitefish light by now. If it was lit.
Seas are coming higher than the pilothouse now, Captain. I've never seen that.
Bridge! We're taking water in the tunnel, it's coming down the... it's over the...
column5: Shouting over machinery. Cuts off mid-word.

column4: Captain, the whole deck's gone under! She's not coming up! She's not...
The National Weather Service has upgraded its gale warning for Lake Superior to a storm warning, with winds to sixty knots and seas of twenty feet or more. All shipping is advised to seek shelter.
In Sault Ste. Marie, the Coast Guard reports several vessels anchored in Whitefish Bay riding out tonight's storm. Power is out across much of the eastern Upper Peninsula.
The forecast for the Soo: snow tonight, heavy at times, with northwest winds gusting past fifty. Temperatures in the twenties. Drive carefully out there.
Okay, it's eight-fifty on your dial, and if you're out on the big lake tonight, friend, this one's for you. Keep her pointed into it.
That was a little something to warm you up. Temperature here at the station is thirty-one degrees and dropping. Snow in the forecast. Who'd have guessed.
If you're hearing this, you're a long way from anywhere. Stay with me. I'll keep the lights on.

Fitzgerald, Coast Guard Sault. Latest from Marquette: winds northwest fifty-five to sixty-five knots, seas eighteen to twenty-five feet, snow, visibility near zero. Storm warning remains in effect. Over.
